implementation_notes: Swift's value types are the memento: copying a struct produces an independent value, so a state struct with value-type members is a complete snapshot and the caretaker is an array with an explicit depth bound - no cloning code at all. Codable plus JSONEncoder/JSONDecoder turns the same struct into a durable memento for autosave or session restore, and the originator applies a snapshot by assigning it, which re-establishes its invariants in one place. A class-based state model instead needs an explicit copy (NSCopying or a copy method), and a struct holding class references remains only shallowly a snapshot. Foundation's UndoManager is the alternative when the platform undo UI (menu titles, groups, responder chain) is the requirement.
pitfalls: A struct snapshot is only deep if its stored properties are value types; a nested class reference is shared with the snapshot and keeps mutating after the save.
Copy-on-write inside Array, Dictionary and String is an optimisation, not a guarantee for custom types - a hand-rolled buffer must call isKnownUniquelyReferenced itself.
Codable round-trips lose anything not encoded (weak references, identity, caches), so rehydration must go through the originator.
An unbounded history array holds whole states; trim it or use a bounded ring buffer.

variants.name: Foundation UndoManager as the caretaker
variants.implementation_notes: Foundation ships a general-purpose caretaker: UndoManager records undo operations with registerUndo(withTarget:handler:) (or the selector/invocation forms), performs undo() and redo(), groups them (beginUndoGrouping/endUndoGrouping, groupsByEvent) and bounds depth with levelsOfUndo. It is operation-based rather than snapshot-based - the registered closure reverses the change - so memento-style undo means capturing a state value in the closure, which pairs naturally with Swift's value-type states. Reach for it when the platform undo infrastructure (menu titles, responder chain, undo grouping, discardable actions) is required; in Swift it is MainActor-isolated, so background actors must hop before registering or performing undo.
pitfalls: UndoManager registers operations, not state: a closure that captures a shared reference instead of a value snapshot undoes to the current state.
It is MainActor-isolated in Swift, so registering from a background actor requires an explicit hop; ignoring this is a concurrency error, not a warning.
levelsOfUndo defaults to unlimited and groupsByEvent groups by run-loop pass, so history can hold far more than intended unless the limit is set.
Undo closures retain their targets until the action is removed; removeAllActions or discardable actions are needed for short-lived editors.
